1:
The claim behind the pomp is read alike by all. John Wesley (wesleyan-arminian) has him act as eldest surviving son, Amnon being dead and Chileab dead or incapable, the display calculated to make the people conclude the succession already settled on him. Adam Clarke (wesleyan-arminian) reproduces Calmet’s character of the man — bold, revengeful, haughty, magnificent, eloquent and popular — who after his brother’s death saw no hindrance to the throne, being royal by both parents, and whose sin was simply that he sought it in his father’s lifetime. Charles Ellicott (grammatical-historical) notes that impressing the people with splendour was a necessary preparation for revolt, as it was afterwards for Adonijah, and that this is the first use in Israel of chariots and horses as regal state. Matthew Henry (puritan-evangelical) sharpens it: the son had learned of the king of Geshur to multiply horses, forbidden to Israel’s kings, so that he looked desirable while his father on a mule looked despicable — the people wanted a king like the nations, and here was one.

At the gate the performance is detailed. John Gill (reformed) has him rise early to show how industrious he would be in office; Wesley reads a show of solicitude for the public and for every private person, forestalling each man with an offer of help. Henry has him out before the king’s other sons were stirring, prying into every man’s city so as to inform himself of the whole kingdom, and embracing whoever offered obeisance while his heart was as proud as Lucifer’s — ambitious projects being often carried on under a show of humility, and fawning on the people to betray them being abominable hypocrisy. Keil and Delitzsch (grammatical-historical) add the classical parallel, that Agamemnon is said to have secured the command of the Grecian army by conduct of just this kind.

On the complaint that no man was deputed to hear causes, they converge on one word for it. Ellicott explains the office first — the king could not hear every case, so appointed men heard causes and reported the facts — then names the art: he does not accuse the king of wrong but insinuates that the system is defective and professes his own wish to set it right, which is what the demagogue has done in every age. Clarke says he was versed in those arts, that the common people heard him gladly, and that like all pretended patriots he found fault with men in power only because he wanted their places, meaning to act as they did or worse. Henry and Wesley make the same observation in nearly the same words, that it is the way of turbulent and aspiring men to reproach the government they are under, and that even David could not escape the worst of censures — Wesley adding the slanders: the other sons and the judges corrupt or careless, the father too old to mind public affairs.

The wish to be judge draws Henry’s hardest sentence. Henry observes that a man who should himself have been judged to death for murder had the impudence to aim at judging others, and that those are commonly most ambitious of preferment who are least fit for it; he adds that the man wanted no subordinate place, though under his own father, but must be supreme or nothing, never considering what a fatigue it would be to have every man come to him, since Moses himself could not bear it. Gill notes that the cause was approved on hearing one side only, Henry that a bad cause can always be given a good colour when its owner tells the story. On the closing phrase Keil and Delitzsch insist it means not to deceive but to steal the heart — to bring a man over secretly and by stratagem.
7:
The forty years are read five ways. Charles Ellicott (grammatical-historical) calls the figure certainly incorrect, since the son was born after his father began to reign and that reign was only forty years, and prefers the four of the Syriac, most Vulgate manuscripts and Josephus. Keil and Delitzsch (grammatical-historical) agree it is altogether unsuitable, fitting neither the son’s age nor any year of the reign, and reject counting from Saul’s accession, as the Rabbins do. John Gill (reformed) canvasses six reckonings — from Israel’s first king, from the slaying of the priests at Nob, from the anointing by Samuel — finds none satisfactory, and is tempted to conclude the copy has forty for four. Adam Clarke (wesleyan-arminian) notes that no Hebrew manuscript yet discovered supports four, and prefers another correction: two of Kennicott’s manuscripts read forty days, which he thinks likelier than the received text. Matthew Henry (puritan-evangelical) and John Wesley (wesleyan-arminian) keep the forty and move the starting point, dating it from the change of the government into a monarchy some ten years before David’s accession, which puts the revolt in his thirtieth year.

Whether the vow was real divides them more simply. Henry suspects none was made, since a man who stuck at neither murder nor treason would not make conscience of a lie, and nobody could disprove him. Wesley has the sacrifices offered in no devotion to God but as a pretence for calling great numbers together, and Clarke notes the pose of a strict worshipper maintained even in a heathen country. Ellicott alone allows the vow may have been genuine, there being nothing improbable in his having made one in exile, however plainly he now uses it as a pretext. On the choice of Hebron they agree: Henry and Wesley make it a royal city in the heart of Judah where his interest was strong and his father’s reign had begun; Keil and Delitzsch and Ellicott add that many there may have resented the removal of the court to Jerusalem.

The machinery of the rising draws Clarke’s sharpest observation: the trumpet served as a kind of telegraph, trumpet exciting trumpet from place to place until in a few minutes all Israel had the proclamation. Ellicott and Keil and Delitzsch stress that the agents were to sound the people first and declare themselves only where they found support.

On the two hundred guests all agree they knew nothing. Gill reports a Jewish tradition that leave was given to invite only two, and that he asked two more unknown to the first, and so on two by two to two hundred. Ellicott takes them for prominent citizens whose ignorance shows how close the secret was kept, and whom their host meant either to win at Hebron or to prevent from opposing him. Henry explains why men known to be loyal were worth inviting: the common people would conclude they had gone over, and the king was deserted by his best friends. He and Wesley then make the same remark in nearly the same words, that it is no new thing for good men and good things to be used by designing men to colour bad practices.

Why the counsellor deserted is the one real conflict. Gill thinks he may have been Bathsheba’s grandfather, resenting the adultery and the death of Uriah. Ellicott sets out the evidence and dismisses it: the names in the two genealogies are not demonstrably one man, and had they been, a grandfather would likelier have felt honoured than aggrieved that his granddaughter was made queen. He proposes instead that this counsellor and many others of Judah were alienated as their relative importance shrank in a growing empire, and notes that the revolt was cradled in Judah. Clarke observes that in gaining him the rebel gained the prime minister.
13:
Adam Clarke (wesleyan-arminian) alone accounts for so general a defection, offering seven reasons: that the king was old and could not attend to justice; that no judges were properly appointed; that Joab’s power had grown oppressive and the king dared not execute the law against him; that partisans of Saul’s house still thought the crown unfairly got; that the king lay under God’s displeasure for Bathsheba and Uriah; that every state has men who can never rest; and that the son was the undisputed heir, most people being readier to hail the rising than the setting sun. John Gill (reformed) notices only that the news came by a messenger, perhaps one of the two hundred who got away when the design appeared.

Why the king fled at all divides them four ways. Clarke says this was the first time David turned his back on an enemy, and finds no military reason for it: the city was so strong that the blind and the lame had once been thought defence enough, and he still had his guard and his six hundred. He reads it instead as submission: the king takes all as from the hand of God, weeps, goes barefoot, covers his head, and does not even hasten, since the habit of mourners is not that of men fleeing before enemies — he sees the storm and yields to what he takes for the tempest of the Almighty. John Wesley (wesleyan-arminian) gives a military reason: Zion was strong but unprovisioned, and once shut in he would have lost the kingdom, where by marching out he could raise an army. Keil and Delitzsch (grammatical-historical) suspect he feared betrayal, and fled to prevent a massacre and give his adherents time to gather. Charles Ellicott (grammatical-historical) judges the course vindicated by the sequel, since both of the rebel’s own counsellors saw that delay would be fatal to an unreasonable cause. On the halting-place he and Keil and Delitzsch agree it is a proper name, the far house, the last on the outskirts before the road crossed the Kidron.

Who the six hundred were is disputed. Keil and Delitzsch call the name strange, since actual Philistines cannot be meant, and hold the apposition to identify them as the old companions in arms who gathered to David in his flight from Saul. Ellicott argues the same, tracing the body through Keilah, the wilderness, Gath, Ziklag and Hebron, and supposing them the later mighty men. Wesley reads it the other way: they were Philistines by birth of the city or territory of Gath, won by David’s counsel and example to the true religion, which is why their leader is called a stranger and they his brethren. Clarke reports that they are generally supposed proselytes, and that some take their leader for a son of the king of Gath, banished for attachment to David. Keil and Delitzsch add that he brought his whole family, and reject Thenius’s view that he came as a hostage as founded on a misreading.

The instruction to go back and abide with the king raises which king is meant, and the two readings are flatly opposed. Wesley takes it of the usurper, now made king, with whom a man whose settled home is in Jerusalem may properly remain. Ellicott denies that David either recognises the son as king or speaks ironically: reading the clause as a stranger and an exile at thy place, he has the king tell a foreigner that the quarrel is no concern of his and that he may serve whoever holds power in fact. Ellicott sets the reply beside Ruth’s. On the parting blessing Wesley takes it for a prayer that God would make good to a true-hearted proselyte the promises given not to Israelites only, and Keil and Delitzsch refer the grace and truth to God’s own.
24:
Why the ark went back is answered five ways. John Gill (reformed) calls the reason not easy to account for, since the thing would fall into the conspirators’ hands, and settles on the king’s trusting that a sacred object would not be violated, and was safest at home; he refuses outright the suggestion of Procopius of Gaza that David could not bear to carry about him a law which accused him of adultery and murder. Adam Clarke (wesleyan-arminian) reads confidence and humility together: the ark was too precious to expose to his wanderings, and he would not carry out of the city of God the one thing without which public worship could not go on, feeling more for that worship than for his own safety. John Wesley (wesleyan-arminian) adds a care for the priests, whom carrying it would have exposed to the rebel’s rage. Charles Ellicott (grammatical-historical) gives the sharpest reason: recognising that he suffers under Nathan’s sentence, the king will not take the ark lest he seem to compel the divine presence and blessing. Keil and Delitzsch (grammatical-historical) say simply that he put his fate into the Lord’s hand.

The priests’ conduct is reported variously. Clarke explains their coming out at all: they knew the kingdom had been given to David and had no evidence he was deposed, so they chose to accompany him with their charge. Ellicott finds the language obscure and reconstructs it, with the one priest and the Levites bringing the ark out and setting it down while the crowd gathered, and the other leading that crowd up the mount; the king addresses the first exclusively and merely mentions the second, which tells us nothing of their standing but much about a day of confusion. Wesley has the high priest go up from the ark toward the city, which lay higher, to use his authority in persuading the people to their duty, and wait until all who would be persuaded had come out.

The address to that priest is a crux. Keil and Delitzsch deny the interrogative can stand, since the question would concern what the man could not have denied, and repoint the word as a vocative, as Jerome and Luther had done: thou seer, seer being equivalent to prophet, applied to a high priest who received divine answers by the Urim — so his proper place was the city. Ellicott allows either rendering, the change being one vowel, and explains the title by the office the man was now to fill in guiding the king’s course and reporting what events showed of God’s will; he adds that neither Nathan nor Gad appears in this narrative, though both were certainly still living. Gill and Wesley take the word in its plainer sense of a discerning man, Wesley adding that this suits the king’s purpose, which needed prudence and secrecy. Clarke gives another ground for sending him back: he was the one organ of public worship, and had nothing to fear personally — for the nation had abandoned their king but not their God.

Two smaller readings close the section. On the place of waiting Ellicott notes that the margin’s plain of the wilderness is followed by the ancient versions, but prefers the text’s the fords, both as a definite place where messengers could find the king and as a position leaving a retreat across the Jordan open. On the covered head Keil and Delitzsch see only grief and mourning, but Clarke notes it was the attitude of a condemned man as well: the heads of culprits were covered when sentence had passed, as with Haman, and a Roman historian records the same order over Philota. Gill identifies the mount from its olive trees, a mile east of the city, and observes that the antitype of David was often there in his own humiliation.
31:
Ahithophel’s name among the conspirators is what alarms the king. Matthew Henry (puritan-evangelical) reckons one good head in such a design worth a thousand good hands: Absalom was himself no politician, but had got entirely into his interest one who was, the more dangerous for having been all along acquainted with David’s counsels and affairs — baffle him and the head of the conspiracy is cut off. Adam Clarke (wesleyan-arminian) agrees the man was well versed in state affairs and that God alone could confound his devices. Henry marks what the prayer does and does not ask: not against the person but against the counsel, that a wise man might for once advise foolishly, or advising wisely be rejected as foolish, or being followed be defeated of his end.

The height where the king halted is a place of worship. Keil and Delitzsch (grammatical-historical) read a sanctuary on the summit of Olivet, probably a bamah of the kind that went on existing round the land even after the temple was built. Charles Ellicott (grammatical-historical) renders the clause where men worship, the original indicating a customary act, and takes it for one of the high places that abounded in Israel. Clarke draws the practical lesson: in danger of his life the king stops to pray, and prayer and provender never hinder any man’s journey. Hushai arrives while the words are still being spoken. Ellicott puts his home on the Ephraim and Benjamin border, supposes him there when the rising broke out, and calls his coming the beginning of the answer to the prayer; Keil and Delitzsch take the title the narrative gives him, the king’s friend, for the office of a privy councillor, and read the rent coat and earth as deepest mourning.

Every witness who touches the counsel David then gives condemns it, and they differ only in what they allow against the verdict. Ellicott says plainly that David here counsels fraud and treachery and that Hushai willingly accepts the part assigned him, the narrative stating the facts without justifying them; he pleads two things — that like frauds in war and rebellion have been practised in all ages and still are, and that David and Hushai had but slender knowledge of the revelation of truth and righteousness which enables us to condemn them, and so did with a clear conscience much we see to be wrong. John Wesley (wesleyan-arminian) is shorter: the crafty counsel must be reckoned among David’s sins, and nevertheless God was pleased to direct the evil advice to a good end. Henry will not have it justified as a stratagem of war at all, and allows only that a son in arms against his father must stand on his guard against all mankind, and if he will be deceived let him be deceived.

Why send the man back rather than keep him? Clarke answers that he was no warrior but wise and discreet, useful for intelligence; Henry adds that the king had now more need of soldiers than of counsellors. The chain runs through the priests. John Gill (reformed) has Zadok and Abiathar assisting to frame schemes directly opposite to Ahithophel’s and placed to pass on what the new court lets slip; Clarke calls it a strict confederacy, their sons serving as couriers between the city and the king’s retreat. Of the closing verse Keil and Delitzsch note that the construction marks the two arrivals as contemporaneous, Hushai entering as Absalom entered. Henry’s comment is on how soon royal cities change their masters; Clarke’s is on the vicissitude of human affairs — the greatest king that ever lived, politician, general, poet and prophet, driven out by his own son and forsaken by his fickle people, proof that none is so exalted that God cannot abase, nor so abased that God cannot exalt.
